k_wheat.name: Growing wheat
k_wheat.desc: Opening the book. A seed needs soil, water and time.
k_wheat.topic: Opening the book. A seed needs soil, water and time; wheat seeds are sown in loose soil, watered, then the stalks grow, turn golden and are cut; each stalk gives grain (to eat or sow) and straw.
k_wheat.page: Every seed needs three things to grow: soil, water and time. Farmers sow wheat seeds in loose soil and water them. The green stalks grow tall, turn golden, and then they are cut. Each stalk gives grain, to eat or to sow again, and a dry stem called straw.

questions.q: What three things does a seed need to grow?
questions.why: With soil, water and enough time, a seed can sprout and grow.

questions.q: How can you tell your wheat is ready to cut?
questions.why: Wheat turns golden when the grain is ripe and ready to harvest.

questions.q: What two things does each wheat stalk give you?
questions.why: The top gives grain to eat or sow, and the dry stem is straw.

k_fire.name: A safe little fire
k_fire.desc: Fire needs three things: fuel, air and heat (fire triangle). Build it inside a ring of stones, start with dry twigs before thicker sticks, never leave it alone, put it out with water or soil.
k_fire.topic: Fire needs three things: fuel, air and heat (fire triangle). Build it inside a ring of stones, start with dry twigs before thicker sticks, never leave it alone, put it out with water or soil.
k_fire.page: A fire needs three things: fuel to burn, air, and heat. Build it inside a ring of stones, and light small dry twigs before you add thicker sticks. Never leave a fire alone. To put it out, pour on water or cover it with soil, which keeps the air away.

questions.q: What three things does every fire need?
questions.why: Take away the fuel, the air or the heat, and the fire goes out.

questions.q: Your big sticks won't catch fire. What should you light first?
questions.why: Small dry twigs catch fire easily and then help the bigger sticks burn.

questions.q: Why does covering a fire with soil put it out?
answers: The soil keeps the air away
The soil makes the fire hotter
The soil burns up like fuel
questions.why: A fire needs air, so covering it with soil makes it go out.

k_roots.name: Roots you can eat
k_roots.desc: Carrots and onions are plants whose roots/bulbs we eat.
k_roots.topic: Carrots and onions are plants whose roots/bulbs we eat; the green leaves above ground make food from sunlight; they grow slower than leafy plants; pull them when the top is big.
k_roots.page: With carrots and onions, we eat the part under the ground: a carrot's root and an onion's round bulb. Their green leaves above the ground use sunlight to make food for the plant. They grow more slowly than leafy plants like lettuce. Pull them up when the green tops are big.

questions.q: Which part of a carrot do we eat?
questions.why: The orange part we eat is the carrot's root, which grows underground.

questions.q: What do the green leaves of a carrot do?
answers: Soak up rain for the root
questions.why: Leaves use sunlight to make food for the whole plant, even the root.

questions.q: How can you tell your carrots are ready to pull?
answers: The leaves are still small and new
questions.why: Big green tops mean the root below has had time to grow big too.

k_rope.name: Twisting rope from fibres
k_rope.desc: Rope is made by twisting plant fibres (from tough weed stems, flax, or straw) into strands and twisting the strands together the other way so the rope does not unwind.
k_rope.topic: Rope is made by twisting plant fibres (from tough weed stems, flax, or straw) into strands and twisting the strands together the other way so the rope does not unwind; more strands = stronger rope.
k_rope.page: Rope is made from fibres, the thin, tough threads inside plant stems like flax or straw. First you twist the fibres into strands. Then you twist the strands together the other way, so the rope does not unwind. The more strands you use, the stronger the rope.

questions.q: Why twist the strands together the other way?
answers: So the rope does not unwind
questions.why: Twisting the opposite way locks the strands, so the rope holds together.

questions.q: You need rope to lift a heavy bucket. What makes it stronger?
questions.why: Each extra strand shares the pull, so the rope gets stronger.

questions.q: What is rope made from?
answers: Thin twigs tied together in knots
questions.why: Fibres from plants like flax or straw are twisted to make rope.

k_tools.name: Stone tools
k_tools.desc: The first tools: a sharp flake of stone becomes a knife.
k_tools.topic: The first tools: a sharp flake of stone becomes a knife; a stone head tied (hafted) to a stick handle with rope becomes an axe; handles make tools stronger by leverage; people used stone tools for a very long time (Stone Age).
k_tools.page: The first tools were made of stone. A sharp flake chipped off a stone makes a knife. Tie a stone to a wooden handle with rope to make an axe; the handle lets you swing much harder. People used stone tools for a very, very long time, called the Stone Age.

questions.q: Why tie a stone axe head onto a handle?
answers: So you can swing much harder
So the stone stays sharp forever
questions.why: A handle works like a longer arm, so each swing hits much harder.

questions.q: How were the very first knives made?
answers: From a sharp flake of stone
From melted iron poured into a mould
questions.why: People chipped a sharp flake off a stone and used it to cut.

questions.q: What do we call the long time when people used stone tools?
questions.why: People used stone tools for so long that we call it the Stone Age.

k_weeds.name: Why weeds come back
k_weeds.desc: Weeds are wild plants that grow where we do not want them.
k_weeds.topic: Weeds are wild plants that grow where we do not want them; they steal water, light and food from crops; their seeds blow in and wait in the soil; pulling them with roots stops them regrowing; borders and mulch help.
k_weeds.page: Weeds are wild plants that grow where we don't want them. They steal water, light and food from our crops. Their seeds blow in on the wind and can wait in the soil for years. Pull weeds out with their roots, and use a border or a cover of straw to keep new ones away.

questions.q: Why are weeds bad for your crops?
answers: They steal water, light and food
They make the soil much too loose
questions.why: Weeds take the water, light and food that your crops need.

questions.q: You pulled a weed, but it grew back. What went wrong?
answers: Its roots stayed in the soil
You pulled it on a sunny day
questions.why: If the roots stay in the ground, the weed can grow again.

questions.q: Your bed is clean now. How can you keep new weeds away?
answers: Water the bare soil every day
questions.why: A straw cover or a border stops many weed seeds from growing.

k_water.name: Water and the well
k_water.desc: A well reaches water stored underground (groundwater) that came from rain soaking into the soil.
k_water.topic: A well reaches water stored underground (groundwater) that came from rain soaking into the soil; a deeper shaft reaches more water; a winch (a roller with a handle) makes lifting the bucket easier.
k_water.page: Rain soaks down through the soil and is stored deep underground. This water is called groundwater. A well is a deep hole that reaches it, and a deeper well reaches more water. A winch, which is a roller with a handle, makes lifting the heavy bucket much easier.

questions.q: Where does the water in a well come from?
answers: Rain that soaked into the ground
The sea, flowing under the farm
Ice melting at the bottom of the hole
questions.why: Rain soaks into the soil and collects deep underground as groundwater.

questions.q: Your well keeps running dry. What could help?
questions.why: A deeper well reaches more of the water stored underground.

questions.q: What does a winch help you do?
questions.why: Turning the winch handle winds up the rope, so lifting is easier.

k_soil.name: Loose soil, happy roots
k_soil.desc: Roots need air and water in the soil.
k_soil.topic: Roots need air and water in the soil; digging loosens hard soil so roots can grow deep and more plants fit in one bed; worms also loosen soil; stamping on beds packs it hard again.
k_soil.page: Roots need air and water in the soil to grow. Digging breaks up hard soil, so roots can grow deep and more plants fit in one bed. Worms help too, because their tunnels loosen the soil. But stamping on a bed packs it hard again.

questions.q: Why do roots grow better in loose soil?
answers: Loose soil is warmer in winter
questions.why: Loose soil has room for air and water, and roots can push down deep.

questions.q: Which little animal helps loosen the soil?
questions.why: Worms dig tunnels as they move, which loosens the soil.

questions.q: Your friend keeps walking on your bed. What happens to the soil?
questions.why: Feet squeeze the soil tight, so roots struggle to grow.

k_ash.name: Ash feeds the soil
k_ash.desc: Wood ash from a fire contains minerals (like potassium) that plants need.
k_ash.topic: Wood ash from a fire contains minerals (like potassium) that plants need; sprinkling a little on beds feeds crops; plants growing close together need more food (fertilizer); too much ash is not good either.
k_ash.page: Wood ash from the fire holds minerals, like potassium, that plants need. Sprinkle a little on your beds to feed your crops. Plants growing close together need extra food, called fertilizer. But be careful: too much ash can harm plants.

questions.q: Why sprinkle wood ash on your beds?
answers: It has minerals that feed plants
It helps the soil hold on to rain
questions.why: Ash holds minerals like potassium, which help plants grow.

questions.q: Your bed is packed with plants. What do they need more of?
questions.why: Many plants close together share the soil's food, so they need extra.

questions.q: How much ash should you put on a bed?
questions.why: A little ash feeds plants, but too much can harm them.

k_chickens.name: Keeping hens
k_chickens.desc: Hens eat grain and seeds, drink water every day, need a dry coop with straw to sleep safe from foxes, and lay eggs.
k_chickens.topic: Hens eat grain and seeds, drink water every day, need a dry coop with straw to sleep safe from foxes, and lay eggs; a hen does not need a rooster to lay eggs; they also scratch for bugs.
k_chickens.page: Hens eat grain and seeds, and they scratch the ground to find bugs. They need fresh water every day and a dry coop with straw, where they sleep safe from foxes. Hens lay eggs, and a hen does not need a rooster to lay them.

questions.q: Where should your hens sleep at night?
answers: In a dry coop with straw
Out in the open field all night
questions.why: A dry coop keeps hens cosy and safe from foxes.

questions.q: Do hens need a rooster to lay eggs?
answers: No, hens lay eggs on their own
Yes, every egg needs a rooster
questions.why: A hen lays eggs whether or not there is a rooster.

questions.q: Why do hens scratch at the ground?
questions.why: Hens scratch the soil to find tasty bugs and seeds.

k_birds.name: Birds, seeds and scarecrows
k_birds.desc: Birds love freshly sown seeds and rabbits nibble young plants.
k_birds.topic: Birds love freshly sown seeds and rabbits nibble young plants; a scarecrow that looks like a person frightens birds; moving or flapping things work better; a fence keeps rabbits out; more plants attract more pests.
k_birds.page: Birds love to eat freshly sown seeds, and rabbits nibble young plants. A scarecrow looks like a person, so it frightens birds, but things that flap or move scare them even better. A fence keeps rabbits out. Remember: the more plants you grow, the more hungry visitors come.

questions.q: Which scarecrow will keep birds away best?
questions.why: Moving, flapping things scare birds better than a scarecrow that never moves.

questions.q: Rabbits keep nibbling your young plants. What helps most?
questions.why: A fence stops rabbits from reaching your plants.

questions.q: You planted twice as many crops. What should you expect?
answers: Fewer birds and rabbits than before
questions.why: More plants mean more food, so more hungry visitors come.

k_grinding.name: Grinding grain into flour
k_grinding.desc: Flour is grain ground into powder between two stones (a quern, later a mill).
k_grinding.topic: Flour is grain ground into powder between two stones (a quern, later a mill); the hard outside (bran) and the inside get crushed; it takes a lot of turning by hand; bread and pancakes need flour.
k_grinding.page: Flour is grain that has been ground into powder. You crush the grain between two heavy stones called a quern; later, people built mills to do it. The hard outside of the grain, called bran, and the soft inside both get crushed. It takes lots of turning by hand, but then you can make bread and pancakes.

questions.q: How is grain turned into flour?
answers: It is crushed between two stones
It is soaked in water for many days
It is dried in the sun
questions.why: Two heavy stones grind the grain until it becomes fine powder.

questions.q: What is bran?
answers: The hard outside of the grain
The soft inside of the grain
questions.why: Bran is the tough outer skin of each grain.

questions.q: Why is making flour by hand hard work?
answers: The stone needs lots of turning
The grain has to be boiled first
questions.why: You turn the quern stone again and again to grind the grain.

k_market.name: Fair prices
k_market.desc: Buying and selling: things that take more work or are rare cost more.
k_market.topic: Buying and selling: things that take more work or are rare cost more; selling something you made from cheaper things adds value; a fair price is good for buyer and seller; money is a way to swap work.
k_market.page: At the market, people buy and sell. Things that are rare, or take lots of work to make, cost more. When you turn cheap things into something better, like flour into bread, it is worth more. A fair price is good for the buyer and the seller, and money is just a handy way to swap work.

questions.q: Why does a loaf of bread cost more than its flour?
questions.why: Turning flour into bread takes work, so the bread is worth more.

questions.q: What makes a price fair?
answers: It is good for buyer and seller
The seller gets as much as possible
questions.why: A fair price is good for both people, so both are happy to trade.

questions.q: Only a few people sell honey. Why does it cost a lot?
questions.why: When something is rare, people pay more for the little there is.

k_timber.name: Logs, planks and grain
k_timber.desc: A log can be split along the grain (the lines of the wood) into planks with an axe and wedges.
k_timber.topic: A log can be split along the grain (the lines of the wood) into planks with an axe and wedges; a saw cuts thinner planks with less waste; wood is strong along the grain; trees take many years to grow.
k_timber.page: Wood has lines running along it, called the grain. With an axe and wedges you can split a log along the grain into planks. A saw cuts thinner planks and wastes less wood. Wood is strongest along the grain, and trees take many years to grow, so never waste it.

questions.q: What is the grain of wood?
answers: The lines that run along it
The little seeds inside a log
questions.why: Grain means the lines in wood, which show the way it splits.

questions.q: Why use a saw for thin planks instead of an axe?
answers: A saw makes the tree grow back
questions.why: A saw cuts neat, thin planks, so more of the log gets used.

questions.q: Why should you never waste wood?
answers: Trees take many years to grow
Wood is much heavier than stone
questions.why: A tree needs many years to grow big enough for planks.

k_clay.name: Clay and bricks
k_clay.desc: Clay is very fine, sticky earth.
k_clay.topic: Clay is very fine, sticky earth; it can be shaped when wet; fired in a hot kiln it turns hard and does not soften in water again (bricks, jars); unfired clay crumbles in rain.
k_clay.page: Clay is very fine, sticky earth that you can shape when it is wet. Unfired clay gets soft in the rain and crumbles. Baked in a very hot oven called a kiln, it turns hard for good, and water can't soften it again. That is how we make bricks and jars.

questions.q: When is clay easiest to shape?
questions.why: Wet clay is soft and sticky, so you can press it into shape.

questions.q: Why are bricks fired in a kiln?
answers: So they stay soft and sticky
So they turn back into earth
questions.why: Firing makes clay hard for good, so water can't soften it.

questions.q: Your unfired clay pot was left out in the rain. What happens?
answers: It bakes as hard as a stone
questions.why: Unfired clay soaks up rain and falls apart.

k_charcoal.name: Charcoal
k_charcoal.desc: Charcoal is wood heated with very little air so it does not burn up.
k_charcoal.topic: Charcoal is wood heated with very little air so it does not burn up; the water and smoke leave and black carbon remains; it burns hotter and cleaner than wood, so smiths and glassmakers use it.
k_charcoal.page: Charcoal is made by heating wood with very little air, so it can't burn up. The water and smoke leave the wood, and the black part that stays behind is called carbon. Charcoal burns hotter and cleaner than wood, so smiths and glassmakers love it.

questions.q: How is charcoal made?
answers: Heating wood with very little air
Burning wood in a big, open bonfire
questions.why: With little air, the wood can't burn away; it turns into black charcoal.

questions.q: Why do smiths use charcoal instead of wood?
questions.why: Charcoal gives a hotter, cleaner fire, which smiths need to work metal.

questions.q: What leaves the wood as it turns into charcoal?
questions.why: Water and smoke escape, and black carbon stays behind.

k_building.name: Walls and roofs
k_building.desc: A building needs a strong base (foundation) so it doesn't sink, walls to carry the roof, and a sloped roof so rain runs off.
k_building.topic: A building needs a strong base (foundation) so it doesn't sink, walls to carry the roof, and a sloped roof so rain runs off; triangles make frames stiff; doors and windows need a beam above them.
k_building.page: A building needs a strong base, called a foundation, so it doesn't sink. The walls hold up the roof, and a sloped roof lets rain run off. Triangles make a wooden frame stiff. Every door and window needs a strong beam above it.

questions.q: Why does a roof slope?
answers: So birds can sit on it
questions.why: On a slope, rain runs down and away instead of soaking in.

questions.q: Which shape makes a wooden frame stiff?
questions.why: A triangle can't be pushed out of shape, so it keeps frames strong.

questions.q: Why does a house need a foundation?
answers: So rain runs off the roof
So the windows let in light
questions.why: The foundation is a strong base that stops the heavy house sinking.

k_thatch.name: Thatching with straw
k_thatch.desc: Thatch is a roof of tightly packed straw or reeds laid in thick layers on a steep roof so rain runs down the outside.
k_thatch.topic: Thatch is a roof of tightly packed straw or reeds laid in thick layers on a steep roof so rain runs down the outside; a good thatched roof lasts many years and keeps a house warm in winter.
k_thatch.page: Thatch is a roof made of straw or reeds, packed tightly in thick layers. It sits on a steep roof, so rain runs down the outside and the inside stays dry. A good thatched roof lasts many years, and it keeps the house warm in winter.

questions.q: Why is a thatched roof built steep?
answers: So snow can sit on top
questions.why: On a steep roof, rain slides down the straw before it can soak in.

questions.q: What is thatch made from?
questions.why: Thatch is thick layers of tightly packed straw or reeds.

questions.q: How does thatch help you in winter?
questions.why: Thick straw traps warm air, like a cosy blanket on the house.

k_compost.name: How compost works
k_compost.desc: Compost is old plants, straw and manure broken down by tiny living things (bacteria, fungi, worms) into dark crumbly soil food.
k_compost.topic: Compost is old plants, straw and manure broken down by tiny living things (bacteria, fungi, worms) into dark crumbly soil food; it needs air and some water; turning the heap speeds it up; it gets warm inside.
k_compost.page: Compost is made when tiny living things, like bacteria, fungi and worms, break down old plants, straw and manure. They turn it all into dark, crumbly food for the soil. The heap needs air and a little water, and turning it with a fork makes it work faster. All their busy work makes the heap warm inside!

questions.q: Who turns old plants into compost?
questions.why: Tiny living things eat the old plants and turn them into compost.

questions.q: Your compost heap is very slow. What can you do?
answers: Cover it with a stone lid
questions.why: Turning lets in air, which helps the tiny living things work faster.

questions.q: Why does a compost heap feel warm inside?
answers: Tiny living things are busy working
The manure was still warm from the animals
questions.why: As bacteria and fungi break things down, they give off heat.

k_bread.name: Why bread rises
k_bread.desc: Sourdough starter is flour and water where wild yeast lives.
k_bread.topic: Sourdough starter is flour and water where wild yeast lives; yeast eats sugar in the flour and makes gas bubbles that make the dough rise; baking in a hot oven sets the bubbles so bread is soft inside.
k_bread.page: A sourdough starter is flour and water where wild yeast lives. Yeast is a tiny living thing that eats the sugar in flour and makes bubbles of gas. The bubbles make the dough rise. A hot oven sets the bubbles in place, so the bread is soft inside.

questions.q: Your bread did not rise. What was missing?
questions.why: Yeast makes the gas bubbles that puff the dough up.

questions.q: How does yeast make dough rise?
answers: It soaks up all the water
questions.why: Yeast eats sugar in the flour and gives off gas, which makes bubbles.

questions.q: Why is baked bread soft and airy inside?
answers: The oven squeezes the air out
questions.why: The hot oven firms the dough around the bubbles, so they stay.

k_stove.name: Cooking on a stove
k_stove.desc: A stove keeps the fire inside a box with a chimney, so heat goes into the pot and smoke goes outside.
k_stove.topic: A stove keeps the fire inside a box with a chimney, so heat goes into the pot and smoke goes outside; it uses less wood than an open fire and is safer; soups and stews simmer slowly.
k_stove.page: A stove keeps the fire inside a box with a chimney. The heat goes into the pot, and the smoke goes out through the chimney. A stove uses less wood than an open fire, and it is safer. It is perfect for soups and stews that simmer, which means bubble gently, for a long time.

questions.q: Where does the smoke from a stove go?
questions.why: The chimney carries smoke up and out of the house.

questions.q: Why cook on a stove instead of an open fire?
answers: It uses less wood and is safer
It needs no fuel or wood at all
questions.why: The boxed-in fire sends its heat into the pot, so less wood is wasted.

questions.q: Your stew should simmer. What should it do?
answers: Bubble gently for a long time
Boil very hard for just one minute
questions.why: To simmer means to bubble gently, so food cooks slowly.

k_cows.name: Cows: grass in, milk out
k_cows.desc: Cows eat grass and clover and chew it again later (chewing the cud, ruminants with a stomach in four parts).
k_cows.topic: Cows eat grass and clover and chew it again later (chewing the cud, ruminants with a stomach in four parts); a cow gives milk after she has a calf; cows drink a lot of water and need a dry barn and bedding.
k_cows.page: Cows eat grass and clover, and their stomach has four parts. Later they bring the food back up and chew it again, which is called chewing the cud. A cow gives milk after she has had a calf. Cows drink lots of water and need a dry barn with bedding.

questions.q: Your cow is lying down, chewing, with no food nearby. What is she doing?
questions.why: Cows bring food back up and chew it again; this is chewing the cud.

questions.q: When does a cow start giving milk?
answers: As soon as she is born
questions.why: Like other mothers, a cow makes milk to feed her calf.

questions.q: How many parts does a cow's stomach have?
questions.why: A cow's stomach has four parts to help break down tough grass.

k_butter.name: Cream into butter
k_butter.desc: Milk has cream (fat) that rises to the top.
k_butter.topic: Milk has cream (fat) that rises to the top; shaking or churning cream makes the fat drops stick together into butter, leaving buttermilk; it takes a lot of churning.
k_butter.page: Fresh milk has cream in it, the fatty part, and it rises to the top. If you shake or churn the cream for a long time, the tiny drops of fat stick together into butter. The thin milk left over is called buttermilk.

questions.q: Where does the cream go in a pail of fresh milk?
questions.why: Cream, the fatty part of milk, rises and can be skimmed off the top.

questions.q: How does churning turn cream into butter?
answers: The cream gets very cold and hard
questions.why: Shaking makes tiny drops of fat bump together and stick into butter.

questions.q: What is left over after making butter?
questions.why: After the butter forms, the thin liquid left behind is buttermilk.

k_bees.name: Bees and flowers
k_bees.desc: Bees collect nectar and pollen from flowers.
k_bees.topic: Bees collect nectar and pollen from flowers; while visiting they carry pollen from flower to flower (pollination) so plants make fruit and seeds; they turn nectar into honey stored in wax combs; bees need water too.
k_bees.page: Bees visit flowers to collect sweet nectar and dusty pollen. They carry pollen from flower to flower, which is called pollination, so plants can make fruit and seeds. Bees turn nectar into honey, store it in wax combs, and need water to drink, too.

questions.q: Why do your apple trees need bees?
answers: Bees carry pollen so fruit can grow
Bees eat the little bugs on the bark
questions.why: Moving pollen between flowers, called pollination, lets plants make fruit and seeds.

questions.q: What do bees make honey from?
questions.why: Bees collect sweet nectar from flowers and turn it into honey.

questions.q: Where do bees store their honey?
questions.why: Bees build combs out of wax and fill them with honey.

k_honey.name: From comb to honey
k_honey.desc: Honeycomb is made of six-sided wax cells filled with honey.
k_honey.topic: Honeycomb is made of six-sided wax cells filled with honey; crushing and straining the comb separates honey from wax; beeswax makes candles and waterproofing; honey does not go bad.
k_honey.page: A honeycomb is made of six-sided wax cells full of honey. Crush the comb and strain it through a cloth: the honey drips out, and the wax stays behind. Beeswax makes candles and keeps things waterproof. Honey keeps for years without going bad.

questions.q: What shape are the cells in a honeycomb?
questions.why: Bees build six-sided wax cells that fit snugly together.

questions.q: How do you get honey out of the comb?
questions.why: Crushing breaks the cells, and straining lets the honey drip out.

questions.q: What can you make with the leftover beeswax?
questions.why: Beeswax makes good candles and can make things waterproof.

k_salt.name: Salt keeps food
k_salt.desc: Salt pulls water out of food, and the tiny germs that spoil food cannot grow without water.
k_salt.topic: Salt pulls water out of food, and the tiny germs that spoil food cannot grow without water; that is why salted, dried and pickled food keeps a long time; salt comes from the sea or from salt mines.
k_salt.page: Food spoils when tiny germs grow in it, and germs need water to grow. Salt pulls the water out of food, so the germs can't grow. That is why salted, dried and pickled foods keep for a long time. Salt comes from the sea or from salt mines.

questions.q: Why does salted food keep for a long time?
questions.why: Without water, the germs that spoil food cannot grow.

questions.q: What do germs need to grow in food?
questions.why: Germs need water, so taking the water away stops them.

questions.q: Where does salt come from?
questions.why: Salt is dried from seawater or dug out of salt mines.

k_mucking.name: Muck and manure
k_mucking.topic: Animals make dung; mixed with old bedding straw it is muck; mucking out keeps animals healthy and clean; rotted manure is rich fertilizer for fields — what is waste for animals is food for plants.
k_mucking.page: Animals make dung, and when it mixes with their old bedding straw we call it muck. Mucking out means cleaning the muck away, and it keeps the animals clean and healthy. Rotted manure is rich food for the fields. What is waste for animals is food for plants!

questions.q: Why do you muck out the barn?
questions.why: Fresh, clean bedding keeps animals healthy and comfortable.

questions.q: What can you do with rotted manure?
questions.why: Rotted manure is rich plant food that helps crops grow.

questions.q: What is muck?
questions.why: Muck is animal dung mixed with the old bedding straw.

k_feed.name: What animals eat
k_feed.desc: Hens eat grain and seeds, cows and sheep eat grass, clover and hay.
k_feed.topic: Hens eat grain and seeds, cows and sheep eat grass, clover and hay; leftover vegetables and pressed seed cake (oilcake) can be feed; animals always need clean water; too much of one food is not healthy.
k_feed.page: Hens eat grain and seeds. Cows and sheep eat grass, clover and hay, which is dried grass. Leftover vegetables and oilcake, the pressed seeds left after making oil, can be feed too. Every animal needs clean water, and too much of one food is not healthy.

questions.q: What do cows and sheep mostly eat?
questions.why: Cows and sheep eat grass and clover, and hay is dried grass.

questions.q: What is oilcake?
answers: Pressed seeds left after making oil
A sweet cake baked for the farm animals
questions.why: After seeds are pressed for oil, the leftover cake makes good feed.

questions.q: Why give your animals a mix of foods?
answers: Too much of one food isn't healthy
Mixed food means they need no water
Mixed food is cheaper to buy
questions.why: Animals stay healthy with a mix of foods and clean water.

k_rotation.name: Crop rotation
k_rotation.desc: Growing the same crop in the same bed again and again tires the soil and invites its pests.
k_rotation.topic: Growing the same crop in the same bed again and again tires the soil and invites its pests; changing crops each time (rotation) helps; beans, peas and clover (legumes) put nitrogen back into the soil.
k_rotation.page: Don't grow the same crop in the same bed year after year. The soil gets tired, and that crop's pests move in. Changing the crop each time is called rotation. Beans, peas and clover are special: they put a plant food called nitrogen back into the soil.

questions.q: What is crop rotation?
answers: Changing the crop in a bed each time
Turning the soil round and round
Planting all your crops in a big circle
questions.why: Rotation means growing a different crop in the bed each time.

questions.q: Which plants put nitrogen back into the soil?
questions.why: Beans, peas and clover add nitrogen, a plant food, to the soil.

questions.q: You grow wheat in the same bed every year. What happens?
answers: The soil tires and pests move in
The wheat grows taller each year
questions.why: One crop again and again tires the soil and feeds the same pests.

k_seasons.name: The four seasons
k_seasons.desc: The year has spring, summer, autumn and winter because the Earth is tilted as it circles the Sun.
k_seasons.topic: The year has spring, summer, autumn and winter because the Earth is tilted as it circles the Sun; in winter days are short and cold so plants grow slowly; spring sprouts, summer ripens, autumn harvests.
k_seasons.page: The year has four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. They happen because the Earth is tilted, or leaning, as it travels around the Sun. In winter the days are short and cold, so plants grow slowly. Seeds sprout in spring, crops ripen in summer, and we harvest in autumn.

questions.q: Why do we have seasons?
answers: The Earth leans as it circles the Sun
The Sun gets bigger in summer
The Earth gets closer to the Sun in summer
questions.why: Because Earth is tilted, our part gets more sunlight in summer and less in winter.

questions.q: Why do plants grow slowly in winter?
answers: The days are short and cold
The soil has no seeds left
questions.why: Plants need light and warmth, and winter has little of both.

questions.q: In which season do farmers harvest most crops?
questions.why: Crops ripen in summer and are gathered in autumn.

k_frost.name: Frost heave: stones that grow
k_frost.desc: Water in the soil freezes and expands in winter, pushing stones upward a little each year (frost heave).
k_frost.topic: Water in the soil freezes and expands in winter, pushing stones upward a little each year (frost heave); farmers find new stones every spring; they piled them into stone walls and paths.
k_frost.page: In winter, water in the soil freezes into ice. Ice takes up more space than water, so it pushes stones up a little every year; this is called frost heave. That is why farmers find new stones every spring. They piled them up to build stone walls and paths.

questions.q: Why do new stones appear in your field each spring?
answers: The stones grew bigger over the winter
questions.why: Frozen water swells and pushes stones a little higher every winter.

questions.q: What happens to water when it freezes?
questions.why: Ice takes up more room than water, so it pushes soil and stones.

questions.q: What did farmers do with all those stones?
questions.why: Farmers piled the stones into walls and paths, so they were useful.

k_pond.name: Ponds and wetlands
k_pond.desc: A pond collects rain and keeps water for dry days.
k_pond.topic: A pond collects rain and keeps water for dry days; ducks, frogs and dragonflies live there; clay at the bottom holds the water in; flax stems are soaked (retted) in ponds to loosen their fibres.
k_pond.page: A pond collects rainwater and keeps it for dry days. Ducks, frogs and dragonflies make their homes there. Clay at the bottom holds the water in, because water can't soak through it. Farmers also soak flax stems in ponds to loosen their fibres, which is called retting.

questions.q: Why does a pond need clay at the bottom?
questions.why: Water can't soak through clay, so it stays in the pond.

questions.q: How does a pond help in a dry summer?
questions.why: A pond stores rainwater, so you still have water when it doesn't rain.

questions.q: Why soak flax stems in a pond?
questions.why: Soaking, called retting, loosens the long fibres inside flax stems.

k_trees.name: Planting trees
k_trees.desc: Trees grow from seeds or young saplings and take years to grow.
k_trees.topic: Trees grow from seeds or young saplings and take years to grow; a woodlot is cut a little at a time and replanted so wood never runs out; fruit trees give fruit every year once grown.
k_trees.page: A tree grows from a seed or from a young tree called a sapling. It takes many years to grow big. In a woodlot, cut just a few trees at a time and plant new ones, so wood never runs out. Once a fruit tree is grown, it gives fruit every year.

questions.q: How can your woodlot never run out of wood?
answers: Cut a few trees and plant new ones
Cut all the trees at once
Only cut the youngest, smallest trees
questions.why: Cutting a little and replanting means new trees are always growing.

questions.q: What is a sapling?
questions.why: A sapling is a young tree, ready to be planted out.

questions.q: Why plant a fruit tree, even though it grows slowly?
questions.why: Once a fruit tree is grown, it gives a harvest year after year.

k_iron.name: Smelting iron
k_iron.desc: Iron ore is rock that contains iron.
k_iron.topic: Iron ore is rock that contains iron; heated very hot with charcoal in a forge, the iron comes out of the rock (smelting); hot iron glows and can be hammered into shape; cold iron is hard and strong.
k_iron.page: Iron ore is a rock with iron hidden inside it. When it is heated very, very hot with charcoal, the iron comes out of the rock; this is called smelting. Hot iron glows and can be hammered into shape. When it cools, iron is hard and strong.

questions.q: What is iron ore?
questions.why: Iron ore is rock that has iron hidden inside.

questions.q: What does smelting mean?
answers: Heating ore so the iron comes out
Hammering hot iron into new shapes
questions.why: Smelting uses great heat and charcoal to get iron out of rock.

questions.q: When is iron easiest to hammer into shape?
questions.why: Glowing hot iron is soft enough to shape; cold iron is hard.

k_smithing.name: Hammer and anvil
k_smithing.desc: A smith heats iron until it glows, then shapes it with a hammer on an anvil.
k_smithing.topic: A smith heats iron until it glows, then shapes it with a hammer on an anvil; dipping hot iron in water (quenching) makes it hard; iron tools last much longer than stone tools.
k_smithing.page: A smith heats iron until it glows, then hammers it into shape on an anvil, a heavy iron block. Dipping the hot tool quickly into water is called quenching, and it makes the tool harder. Iron tools last much longer than stone tools.

questions.q: What is an anvil?
answers: A heavy iron block to hammer on
A big hammer for hitting iron
A bucket of cold water for cooling
questions.why: The smith lays hot iron on the anvil and hammers it into shape.

questions.q: Why does a smith dip a hot tool into water?
questions.why: Cooling it quickly in water, called quenching, makes the tool harder.

questions.q: Why swap your stone axe for an iron one?
questions.why: Iron is tough and lasts far longer than stone, which chips and breaks.

k_nails.name: Nails and joints
k_nails.topic: Nails hold wooden boards together; before nails people cut joints that fit together like puzzles and used wooden pegs; a saw makes straight, thin planks for building.
k_nails.page: Nails hold wooden boards together. Before people had nails, they cut joints: ends that fit together like puzzle pieces. They held the joints tight with wooden pegs. A saw makes straight, thin planks that are good for building.

questions.q: How did people join wood before they had nails?
questions.why: Cut joints fit snugly together, and wooden pegs held them tight.

questions.q: What do nails do?
questions.why: A nail goes through one board into another and holds them together.

questions.q: Why use a saw to make planks for building?
questions.why: Straight, even planks fit together neatly when you build.

k_wind.name: Wind power
k_wind.desc: Moving air (wind) pushes the sails of a windmill round.
k_wind.topic: Moving air (wind) pushes the sails of a windmill round; the turning shaft drives gears that turn heavy millstones; wind power grinds flour or pumps water without people or animals turning it.
k_wind.page: Wind is moving air, and it pushes the sails of a windmill round and round. The sails turn a shaft, which is a long pole, and the shaft drives gears that turn heavy millstones. That way, wind can grind flour or pump water, with no people or animals doing the turning.

questions.q: What makes windmill sails turn?
questions.why: Wind is moving air, and it pushes the sails round.

questions.q: How do the sails turn the heavy millstones?
questions.why: The sails spin a shaft, and gears pass the turning to the stones.

questions.q: Why build a windmill instead of grinding by hand?
answers: The wind does the hard turning
It grinds best with no wind
questions.why: A windmill uses wind power, so people and animals don't have to turn the stones.

k_irrigation.name: Channels and irrigation
k_irrigation.desc: Irrigation brings water to crops through channels or pipes.
k_irrigation.topic: Irrigation brings water to crops through channels or pipes; water flows downhill; watering at the roots wastes less than splashing leaves; a watering can with a spout aims water at the roots.
k_irrigation.page: Irrigation means bringing water to crops through channels or pipes. Water always flows downhill, so the channel must slope down toward the crops. Watering at the roots wastes less water than splashing the leaves. A watering can with a long spout helps you aim right at the roots.

questions.q: Your field is higher than the pond. Why won't channel water reach it?
questions.why: Water flows downhill, so it can't climb up to a higher field.

questions.q: Where is the best place to pour water on a plant?
questions.why: Water at the roots goes where the plant drinks, with less waste.

questions.q: Why does a watering can have a long spout?
answers: To aim water at the roots
questions.why: The spout lets you pour exactly where the roots are.

k_wool.name: Shearing and spinning
k_wool.desc: Sheep grow thick wool that is cut off (sheared) once a year, which doesn't hurt them.
k_wool.topic: Sheep grow thick wool that is cut off (sheared) once a year, which doesn't hurt them; wool is cleaned, combed and twisted on a spindle into yarn; spinning makes long strong threads from short fibres.
k_wool.page: Sheep grow thick wool, and once a year it is cut off. This is called shearing, and it doesn't hurt, just like a haircut. The wool is cleaned, combed and twisted on a spindle into yarn. Spinning turns short, fluffy fibres into long, strong thread.

questions.q: Does shearing hurt a sheep?
answers: No, it is like a haircut
questions.why: Wool is like hair, so cutting it off doesn't hurt the sheep.

questions.q: What does spinning do to wool?
answers: Makes long thread from short fibres
Washes all the dirt and grease out of it
questions.why: Twisting short fibres on a spindle joins them into one long, strong yarn.

questions.q: How often are sheep sheared?
questions.why: Sheep grow a thick new coat each year, so they are sheared once a year.

k_weaving.name: Warp and weft
k_weaving.desc: Cloth is woven on a loom: long threads (the warp) are stretched tight and another thread (the weft) goes over and under them, back and forth.
k_weaving.topic: Cloth is woven on a loom: long threads (the warp) are stretched tight and another thread (the weft) goes over and under them, back and forth; tighter weaving makes stronger cloth.
k_weaving.page: Cloth is woven on a loom. Long threads called the warp are stretched tight. Another thread, the weft, goes over and under them, back and forth, back and forth. The tighter the weaving, the stronger the cloth.

questions.q: What is stretched tight on the loom?
questions.why: The warp is stretched tight first, and the weft weaves through it.

questions.q: How does the weft thread move?
answers: Over and under, back and forth
Round and round in little circles
questions.why: The weft goes over one warp thread and under the next, row after row.

questions.q: You want strong cloth for a grain sack. How should you weave?
questions.why: Tight weaving packs the threads close, which makes strong cloth.

k_flax.name: Flax to linen
k_flax.desc: Flax is a plant with long fibres inside its stem.
k_flax.topic: Flax is a plant with long fibres inside its stem; the stems are soaked (retted) so the fibres loosen, then beaten and combed, spun into thread and woven into linen; flax seeds give linseed oil.
k_flax.page: Flax is a plant with long fibres inside its stem. The stems are soaked until the fibres come loose, which is called retting. Then the fibres are beaten, combed, spun into thread and woven into linen cloth. Flax seeds give linseed oil.

questions.q: What cloth is made from flax?
questions.why: Flax fibres are spun and woven into linen.

questions.q: Why are flax stems soaked first?
answers: To make the seeds inside sprout
questions.why: Soaking, or retting, loosens the long fibres from the stem.

questions.q: What do flax seeds give us?
questions.why: Flax seeds are pressed to make linseed oil.

k_press.name: Pressing oil and juice
k_press.desc: A press squeezes fruit or seeds very hard with a big screw.
k_press.topic: A press squeezes fruit or seeds very hard with a big screw; apples give juice, sunflower and flax seeds give oil; what is left (pomace, oilcake) can feed animals or the compost.
k_press.page: A press squeezes fruit or seeds very hard when you turn its big wooden screw. Apples give juice, and sunflower and flax seeds give oil. What is left over, called pomace or oilcake, can feed animals or go on the compost.

questions.q: What comes out when you press apples?
questions.why: Squeezing apples hard pushes out their sweet juice.

questions.q: What can you do with the leftover oilcake?
questions.why: Leftovers from pressing still have goodness, so animals can eat them.

questions.q: How does a press squeeze so hard?
answers: By heating it in the oven
questions.why: Turning a big screw pushes the press down with great force.

k_sugar.name: Sugar from beets
k_sugar.desc: Sugar beets store sugar in their roots.
k_sugar.topic: Sugar beets store sugar in their roots; the juice is pressed out and boiled so the water evaporates and sugar crystals remain; honey was the main sweetener before sugar was common.
k_sugar.page: Sugar beets store sugar in their big roots. Their juice is squeezed out and boiled, so the water goes off as steam and sugar crystals are left behind. Before sugar was common, people sweetened their food mostly with honey.

questions.q: Where does a sugar beet store its sugar?
questions.why: Sugar beets keep their sugar in their big white roots.

questions.q: Why boil the beet juice?
questions.why: Boiling drives off the water, leaving sugar crystals behind.

questions.q: How did people sweeten food before sugar was common?
questions.why: Honey was the main sweetener long before sugar was easy to get.

k_ferment.name: Friendly microbes
k_ferment.desc: Fermentation: tiny living things (yeasts and bacteria) change food.
k_ferment.topic: Fermentation: tiny living things (yeasts and bacteria) change food; yeast turns apple juice sugar into cider; bacteria turn milk into yogurt; the right microbes keep the bad ones away, so food keeps longer.
k_ferment.page: Microbes are tiny living things, too small to see, like yeasts and bacteria. Some of them change food in a good way, which is called fermentation. Yeast turns the sugar in apple juice into cider, and bacteria turn milk into yogurt. These good microbes keep the bad ones away, so the food keeps longer.

questions.q: What turns apple juice into cider?
questions.why: Yeast eats the sugar in apple juice and turns it into cider.

questions.q: What turns milk into yogurt?
questions.why: Friendly bacteria change milk into thick, tangy yogurt.

questions.q: Why does fermented food keep longer?
answers: Good microbes keep bad ones away
It is kept in the hot sun
All the germs have been boiled away
questions.why: Friendly microbes fill the food, so spoiling germs can't take over.

k_cheese.name: Making cheese
k_cheese.desc: Cheese: milk is thickened (curdled) with cultures and rennet into curds and whey.
k_cheese.topic: Cheese: milk is thickened (curdled) with cultures and rennet into curds and whey; curds are pressed into a wheel; aging in a cool cellar gives stronger taste; ten litres of milk make about one kilo of cheese.
k_cheese.page: To make cheese, you thicken milk with cultures, which are friendly bacteria, and rennet. The milk splits into soft lumps called curds and a watery liquid called whey. The curds are pressed into a round wheel and aged in a cool cellar, which makes the taste stronger. Ten litres of milk make only about one kilo of cheese.

questions.q: When milk thickens for cheese, what does it split into?
questions.why: The soft lumps are curds, and the watery part is whey.

questions.q: How can you make a cheese taste stronger?
answers: Age it in a cool cellar
Add lots more water to it
questions.why: Aging slowly in a cool cellar gives cheese a stronger taste.

questions.q: How much milk makes about one kilo of cheese?
questions.why: Most of the milk drains away as whey, so it takes about ten litres.

k_cellar.name: The cool cellar
k_cellar.desc: Cold slows down the germs that spoil food.
k_cellar.topic: Cold slows down the germs that spoil food; a cellar dug into the ground stays cool and dark all year; potatoes, carrots, apples and cheese keep for months there; dry, dark and cool is the rule.
k_cellar.page: Cold slows down the germs that spoil food. A cellar dug into the ground stays cool and dark all year, even in summer. Potatoes, carrots, apples and cheese can keep there for months. Cool and dark is the rule!

questions.q: Why does food keep longer in a cool cellar?
questions.why: Germs that spoil food work much more slowly in the cold.

questions.q: Why does a cellar stay cool, even in summer?
answers: It is dug into the ground
It is next to the stove
questions.why: Deep in the ground, the temperature stays cool all year round.

questions.q: Which foods can keep in a cellar for months?
questions.why: Hardy foods like potatoes, carrots, apples and cheese last for months in a cellar.

k_pickling.name: Pickling and vinegar
k_pickling.desc: Vinegar is made when bacteria turn cider into acid.
k_pickling.topic: Vinegar is made when bacteria turn cider into acid; vegetables kept in vinegar and salt (pickles) do not spoil because germs can't live in acid; people pickled food for winter and long sea voyages.
k_pickling.page: Vinegar is made when bacteria turn cider into a sour acid. Vegetables kept in vinegar and salt are called pickles. They don't spoil, because the germs that spoil food can't live in sour acid. People pickled food for the winter and for long trips at sea.

questions.q: How is vinegar made?
answers: Salt is stirred into hot water
questions.why: Special bacteria change cider into sour vinegar.

questions.q: Why don't pickles spoil?
answers: Spoiling germs can't live in acid
The jars are kept in the warm sun all day
questions.why: The sour vinegar stops the germs that would spoil the vegetables.

questions.q: Why did sailors take pickles on long sea trips?
answers: Pickles keep for a long time
Pickles are very light to carry
questions.why: Pickled food doesn't spoil, so it lasts through long voyages.

k_double_dig.name: Double digging
k_double_dig.desc: Double digging loosens the soil two spade-depths deep and mixes compost in, so roots go deeper and more plants fit.
k_double_dig.topic: Double digging loosens the soil two spade-depths deep and mixes compost in, so roots go deeper and more plants fit; it is hard work done once, then the bed stays loose for years if you don't step on it.
k_double_dig.page: Double digging means loosening the soil two spade-depths deep and mixing in compost. Then roots can grow deeper, and more plants fit in the bed. It is hard work, but you only do it once. If you never step on the bed, it stays loose for years.

questions.q: How deep do you loosen the soil when double digging?
questions.why: Double digging loosens the soil two spade-blades deep.

questions.q: Why is double digging worth the hard work?
answers: Roots go deeper and more plants fit
Weeds can never, ever grow there again
You never need to water again
questions.why: Deep, loose soil with compost lets roots go down, so plants can grow closer.

questions.q: How do you keep a double-dug bed loose for years?
questions.why: Feet pack the soil hard, so walk on the paths instead.

k_pests.name: Pests and their enemies
k_pests.desc: Slugs, caterpillars, mice and birds eat crops.
k_pests.topic: Slugs, caterpillars, mice and birds eat crops; ladybirds eat aphids, owls and cats catch mice, ducks eat slugs; a garden with many different plants has more pest-eaters; more crops attract more pests.
k_pests.page: Slugs, caterpillars, mice and birds all like to eat our crops. But pests have enemies: ladybirds eat aphids (tiny green bugs), owls and cats catch mice, and ducks gobble up slugs. A garden with many different plants has more of these helpers. And remember, more crops bring more pests.

questions.q: Slugs are eating your lettuce. Which helper could you bring?
questions.why: Ducks love to eat slugs.

questions.q: What do ladybirds eat?
questions.why: Ladybirds gobble up aphids, tiny bugs that harm plants.

questions.q: Why grow many different kinds of plants?
answers: They make crops grow twice as fast
questions.why: Many kinds of plants give homes to ladybirds, birds and other helpers.

k_steel.name: From iron to steel
k_steel.desc: Steel is iron with a tiny bit of carbon (from charcoal) mixed in.
k_steel.topic: Steel is iron with a tiny bit of carbon (from charcoal) mixed in; it is harder and springier than iron, keeps a sharp edge and doesn't break easily; making it needs a very hot furnace.
k_steel.page: Steel is iron with a tiny bit of carbon mixed in, and the carbon comes from charcoal. Steel is harder and springier than iron. It keeps a sharp edge and doesn't break easily. Making steel needs a very hot furnace.

questions.q: What is steel made of?
answers: Iron with a tiny bit of carbon
Iron mixed with lots of sand
questions.why: Adding a tiny bit of carbon from charcoal turns iron into steel.

questions.q: Why make a knife from steel instead of iron?
questions.why: Steel is harder and springier, so its edge stays sharp.

questions.q: Where does the carbon in steel come from?
questions.why: Charcoal is mostly carbon, and a little mixes into the hot iron.

k_glass.name: Sand into glass
k_glass.desc: Glass is made by melting sand in a very hot furnace until it flows like honey, then shaping it and letting it cool slowly.
k_glass.topic: Glass is made by melting sand in a very hot furnace until it flows like honey, then shaping it and letting it cool slowly; it lets light through but keeps wind and rain out.
k_glass.page: Glass is made by melting sand, with a little plant ash to help, in a very hot furnace. Melted glass flows like honey, so it can be shaped. Then it must cool slowly, or it may crack. Glass lets light through but keeps the wind and rain out.

questions.q: What is glass mainly made from?
questions.why: Sand melted in a very hot furnace becomes glass.

questions.q: Why must new glass cool slowly?
questions.why: Cooling too fast can crack glass, so it is cooled slowly.

questions.q: Why put glass in a window?
answers: It lets light in and keeps rain out
It lets the fresh breeze blow through
questions.why: Glass is clear, so light comes in while wind and rain stay out.

k_greenhouse.name: Greenhouses
k_greenhouse.desc: Sunlight shines through glass and warms the air and soil inside.
k_greenhouse.topic: Sunlight shines through glass and warms the air and soil inside; the glass keeps the warm air in, so plants grow even when it's cold outside; people grow tender plants and early seedlings in greenhouses.
k_greenhouse.page: In a greenhouse, sunlight shines through the glass and warms the air and soil inside. The glass keeps the warm air in, so plants can grow even when it is cold outside. People grow tender plants there, which are plants that don't like cold. They also start early seedlings in spring.

questions.q: Why is it warm inside a greenhouse?
answers: Sun warms it and glass keeps heat in
A fire burns under the floor
The plants breathe out lots of hot air
questions.why: Sunlight shines in through the glass, and the glass keeps the warm air inside.

questions.q: What are tender plants?
answers: Plants that are soft to eat
questions.why: Tender plants get hurt by cold, so a greenhouse keeps them safe.

questions.q: It is still chilly in early spring. Where can you start seedlings?
questions.why: A greenhouse is warm and bright, just right for young seedlings.

k_masonry.name: Brick houses
k_masonry.desc: Bricks are laid in rows with mortar between them, each row overlapping the joints below (a bond) so the wall is strong.
k_masonry.topic: Bricks are laid in rows with mortar between them, each row overlapping the joints below (a bond) so the wall is strong; brick walls don't burn or rot and keep a house warm.
k_masonry.page: Bricks are laid in rows with mortar, a sticky paste that dries hard, between them. Each row overlaps the joins in the row below. This pattern is called a bond, and it makes the wall strong. Brick walls don't burn or rot, and they keep a house warm.

questions.q: Why does each row of bricks overlap the row below?
answers: It makes the wall look red
questions.why: Overlapping, called a bond, ties the bricks together so the wall stays strong.

questions.q: What goes between the bricks?
questions.why: Mortar is a paste that sticks the bricks together and dries hard.

questions.q: Why build with bricks instead of wood?
questions.why: Fired clay bricks can't catch fire or rot like wood can.

k_orchard.name: Caring for fruit trees
k_orchard.desc: Fruit trees are pruned in winter: cutting out old and crossing branches lets in light and air so the tree makes better fruit.
k_orchard.topic: Fruit trees are pruned in winter: cutting out old and crossing branches lets in light and air so the tree makes better fruit; bees pollinate the blossoms in spring; apples ripen in autumn.
k_orchard.page: Fruit trees are pruned, or trimmed, in winter. Cutting out old branches and branches that cross lets light and air into the tree, so it makes better fruit. In spring, bees pollinate the blossoms, and in autumn the apples are ripe.

questions.q: Why cut out crossing branches?
answers: To let in light and air
questions.why: With more light and air inside, the tree grows better fruit.

questions.q: When do you prune fruit trees?
questions.why: Fruit trees are pruned in winter, before the spring blossoms come.

questions.q: Who helps the apple blossoms turn into apples?
questions.why: Bees carry pollen between blossoms, which lets apples grow.

k_olives.name: Olives: oil and curing
k_olives.desc: Olives straight from the tree are too bitter to eat.
k_olives.topic: Olives straight from the tree are too bitter to eat; they are cured in salt water for weeks to become tasty; pressed olives give olive oil; olive trees can live for hundreds of years.
k_olives.page: Olives picked straight from the tree taste far too bitter to eat. They are cured, which means soaked in salty water for weeks, until they taste good. Pressed olives give us olive oil. Olive trees can live for hundreds of years.

questions.q: Why are fresh olives soaked in salty water?
answers: They are too bitter to eat
They are too sweet to eat
They are too dry to eat
questions.why: Weeks of soaking in salty water, called curing, takes the bitterness away.

questions.q: How long can an olive tree live?
questions.why: Olive trees grow slowly and can live for hundreds of years.

questions.q: What do you get when you press olives?
questions.why: Pressing squeezes the oil out of olives.

k_pasta.name: Pasta and dough
k_pasta.desc: Pasta is flour and egg (or water) kneaded into a dough, rolled thin and cut.
k_pasta.topic: Pasta is flour and egg (or water) kneaded into a dough, rolled thin and cut; kneading makes the dough stretchy (gluten); fresh pasta cooks in a few minutes in boiling water.
k_pasta.page: Pasta is flour and egg, or flour and water, kneaded into a dough. Kneading means pressing and folding, and it builds gluten, which makes the dough stretchy. The dough is rolled thin and cut into shapes. Fresh pasta cooks in just a few minutes in boiling water.

questions.q: What makes pasta dough stretchy?
questions.why: Kneading builds gluten, which makes the dough stretchy.

questions.q: What is pasta dough made from?
questions.why: Pasta needs just flour and eggs, or flour and water.

questions.q: How long does fresh pasta take to cook?
questions.why: Fresh pasta is thin, so boiling water cooks it in minutes.

k_hardwood.name: Hardwood and joinery
k_hardwood.desc: Hardwoods like oak and beech come from broad-leaved trees that grow slowly.
k_hardwood.topic: Hardwoods like oak and beech come from broad-leaved trees that grow slowly; their wood is dense and strong, good for tools, barrels and machine parts; softwoods from conifers grow faster.
k_hardwood.page: Hardwoods like oak and beech come from trees with broad, flat leaves, and they grow slowly. Their wood is heavy and strong, so it is good for tools, barrels and machine parts. Softwoods come from conifers, trees with needles and cones like pines, and they grow faster.

questions.q: Why make a barrel from oak?
answers: Oak wood is heavy and strong
Oak wood is soft and light
questions.why: Slow-growing hardwoods like oak make heavy, strong wood.

questions.q: Which trees give softwood?
questions.why: Softwoods come from conifers, the trees with needles and cones.

questions.q: Which kind of tree grows faster?
questions.why: Conifers like pine grow faster than hardwoods like oak and beech.

k_deep_soil.name: Deep soil and humus
k_deep_soil.desc: Humus is the dark, rotted part of soil made from old plants.
k_deep_soil.topic: Humus is the dark, rotted part of soil made from old plants; it holds water like a sponge and feeds plants slowly; deep, humus-rich soil lets many plants grow close together.
k_deep_soil.page: Humus is the dark, rotted part of soil, made from old plants. It holds water like a sponge and feeds plants slowly. In deep soil full of humus, many plants can grow close together.

questions.q: What is humus made from?
questions.why: Humus forms when old plants rot down into dark soil.

questions.q: How is humus like a sponge?
questions.why: Humus soaks up water and keeps it for plant roots.

questions.q: Why can many plants grow close in deep, humus-rich soil?
answers: There is plenty of water and food
Stones in the soil keep roots warm
questions.why: Deep soil with humus holds lots of water and food for many roots.

k_mulch.name: Mulching
k_mulch.desc: Mulch is a blanket of straw, leaves or wood chips on top of the soil.
k_mulch.topic: Mulch is a blanket of straw, leaves or wood chips on top of the soil; it keeps moisture in, keeps weeds down (they get no light), protects soil from frost and slowly turns into humus.
k_mulch.page: Mulch is a blanket of straw, leaves or wood chips laid on top of the soil. It keeps water in the ground and stops weeds, because they get no light. It protects the soil from frost. Slowly, the mulch rots and turns into humus.

questions.q: How does mulch stop weeds?
answers: It makes the soil too hot
It makes the soil too wet
questions.why: Under thick mulch, weed seeds get no light, so they can't grow.

questions.q: It's a hot, dry week. How does mulch help?
answers: It keeps water in the soil
It makes rain fall more often
questions.why: Mulch covers the soil like a blanket, so less water dries up.

questions.q: What happens to old mulch over time?
questions.why: Mulch slowly rots down and becomes humus that feeds the soil.

k_dyes.name: Dyes from plants
k_dyes.desc: Many plants give colour: beets and madder red, onion skins yellow, woad blue.
k_dyes.topic: Many plants give colour: beets and madder red, onion skins yellow, woad blue; the plant is boiled in water, then yarn is soaked in the dye bath; a fixing step (mordant) makes the colour stay.
k_dyes.page: Many plants give colour: madder roots and beets make red, onion skins make yellow, and woad makes blue. You boil the plant in water to make a dye bath, then soak the yarn in it. Adding a fixer, called a mordant, makes the colour stay.

questions.q: Which plant gives a blue dye?
questions.why: Woad leaves make a blue dye.

questions.q: You want yellow yarn. What should you boil?
questions.why: Onion skins make a warm yellow dye.

questions.q: Your dyed yarn faded when washed. What did you forget?
questions.why: A mordant fixes the dye, so the colour stays when washed.

k_colour_mixing.name: Mixing colours
k_colour_mixing.desc: Primary dye colours red, yellow and blue mix into secondary colours: red + yellow = orange, yellow + blue = green, red + blue = purple.
k_colour_mixing.topic: Primary dye colours red, yellow and blue mix into secondary colours: red + yellow = orange, yellow + blue = green, red + blue = purple; mixing all three makes brown.
k_colour_mixing.page: Red, yellow and blue are the main dye colours. Mix two of them to make a new colour. Red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, and red and blue make purple. Mix all three together and you get brown.

questions.q: Which two dye colours make green?
questions.why: Yellow mixed with blue gives green.

questions.q: You mix red and blue dye. What colour do you get?
questions.why: Red and blue together make purple.

questions.q: You pour red, yellow and blue together. What colour now?
questions.why: Mixing all three main colours makes brown.

k_worms.name: Worms make soil
k_worms.desc: Earthworms eat dead leaves and compost and leave behind castings, the richest soil food.
k_worms.topic: Earthworms eat dead leaves and compost and leave behind castings, the richest soil food; their tunnels let air and water into the soil; a worm bin turns kitchen scraps into castings.
k_worms.page: Earthworms eat dead leaves and compost. What they leave behind is called castings, and it is the richest food for soil. Their tunnels let air and water into the ground. In a worm bin, worms turn kitchen scraps into castings.

questions.q: What are worm castings?
answers: What worms leave behind after eating
Little worm eggs in the soil
questions.why: Castings are worm droppings, and they are very rich food for plants.

questions.q: How do worm tunnels help your plants?
answers: They let air and water in
They catch the slugs at night
questions.why: Tunnels make paths for air and water to reach the roots.

questions.q: What does a worm bin do with kitchen scraps?
questions.why: Worms eat the scraps and leave castings, a rich food for soil.

k_seed_saving.name: Saving seeds
k_seed_saving.desc: Heirloom plants grow true from their own seeds: let the best plants flower, collect the dry seeds, keep them cool and dry for next year.
k_seed_saving.topic: Heirloom plants grow true from their own seeds: let the best plants flower, collect the dry seeds, keep them cool and dry for next year; seed libraries share old varieties so they don't disappear.
k_seed_saving.page: Heirloom plants are old kinds that grow true from their own seeds: the new plants come out just like the parent. Let your best plants flower, and collect the seeds when they are dry. Keep them cool and dry until next year. Seed libraries share old kinds of seeds, so they don't disappear.

questions.q: Which plants should you save seeds from?
questions.why: Seeds from your best plants grow into good plants too.

questions.q: How should you store saved seeds?
questions.why: Cool, dry seeds stay healthy until planting time next year.

questions.q: Why do seed libraries share old seeds?
answers: So old seeds can be thrown away
questions.why: When many people grow old kinds, those plants stay alive for the future.

k_saffron.name: Saffron, the precious spice
k_saffron.desc: Saffron comes from the three red threads (stigmas) inside each crocus flower, picked by hand.
k_saffron.topic: Saffron comes from the three red threads (stigmas) inside each crocus flower, picked by hand; it takes about 150 flowers for one gram, which is why it is so precious; it colours food golden.
k_saffron.page: Saffron comes from a purple crocus flower. Inside each flower are three red threads, called stigmas, and they are picked by hand. It takes about 150 flowers to make just one gram, so saffron is very precious. A pinch colours food a golden yellow.

questions.q: Why does saffron cost so much?
answers: It grows on big, tall trees
questions.why: About 150 flowers, all picked by hand, make just one gram.

questions.q: Which part of the crocus is saffron?
questions.why: Saffron is the three red threads, called stigmas, in each flower.

questions.q: What does a pinch of saffron do to rice?
questions.why: Just a pinch of saffron turns food a golden yellow.

k_master_baking.name: Master baking
k_master_baking.desc: Fine flour is ground twice and sifted for light cakes.
k_master_baking.topic: Fine flour is ground twice and sifted for light cakes; eggs trap air when beaten; butter and sugar creamed together make cakes soft; an even oven temperature bakes the inside before the outside burns.
k_master_baking.page: For light cakes, flour is ground twice and sifted until it is very fine. Beating eggs traps tiny air bubbles. Creaming, or beating, butter and sugar together makes a cake soft. The oven must be evenly hot, not too hot, so the inside bakes before the outside burns.

questions.q: Why beat the eggs for a cake?
answers: To warm them up for the oven
questions.why: Beaten eggs hold air, which makes the cake light.

questions.q: Your cake burned outside but stayed raw inside. Why?
answers: The eggs were beaten too long
questions.why: Steady, gentle heat lets the middle bake before the outside burns.

questions.q: How do you make flour fine enough for light cakes?
answers: Grind it twice and sift it
Mix in plenty of coarse bran
questions.why: Grinding twice and sifting makes very fine flour for light cakes.

k_wind_pump.name: Pumping water with wind
k_wind_pump.desc: A wind pump uses the turning sails to move a pump rod up and down, lifting water from deep underground into a tank, day and night whenever the wind blows — without anyone pumping by hand.
k_wind_pump.topic: A wind pump uses the turning sails to move a pump rod up and down, lifting water from deep underground into a tank, day and night whenever the wind blows — without anyone pumping by hand.
k_wind_pump.page: A wind pump uses its turning sails to move a pump rod up and down. Each stroke lifts water from deep underground into a tank. It works day and night, whenever the wind blows, with nobody pumping by hand.

questions.q: What makes a wind pump work?
questions.why: The wind spins the sails, and that drives the pump.

questions.q: How does a wind pump lift water?
answers: A rod moves up and down
questions.why: The sails move a pump rod up and down, lifting water each time.

questions.q: When does a wind pump fill the tank?
questions.why: It runs whenever there is wind, even at night.

k_living_soil.name: Living soil
k_living_soil.desc: A spoonful of healthy soil holds billions of tiny living things — bacteria, fungi, worms.
k_living_soil.topic: A spoonful of healthy soil holds billions of tiny living things — bacteria, fungi, worms; fungi threads help roots find water; feeding the soil with compost and not digging it too much keeps it alive.
k_living_soil.page: Healthy soil is alive! One spoonful holds billions of tiny living things, like bacteria and fungi, and worms live there too. Fungi grow long, thin threads that help roots find water. Feed the soil with compost and don't dig it too much, and it stays alive.

questions.q: How many tiny living things are in a spoonful of healthy soil?
questions.why: Healthy soil is packed with billions of tiny living things.

questions.q: How do fungi help plant roots?
answers: Their threads help roots find water
They scare away the slugs and snails
questions.why: Long, thin fungus threads reach far and help roots get water.

questions.q: How can you keep your soil alive?
answers: Add compost and dig only a little
Dig it up deeply every single week
questions.why: Compost feeds the soil life, and too much digging disturbs it.

k_seeds.name: Saving seed
k_seeds.desc: A grain you keep back is a seed you can sow again.
k_seeds.topic: Every grain of wheat can grow into a new plant; a farmer keeps some of the harvest back as seed before eating or selling the rest; one plant gives many grains, so a little seed grows into a lot of food.
k_seeds.page: A grain of wheat is a seed. If you plant it, it grows into a plant, and that plant gives you many new grains. A good farmer always keeps some grains back to sow next time, before eating or selling the rest. That is how one little stalk can become a whole field.

questions.q: What is a grain of wheat?
questions.why: A grain is the seed of the wheat plant: planted, it grows into a new plant.

questions.q: Why does a farmer keep some grains back?
questions.why: Kept grains are the seed for the next sowing. Without them nothing can be planted.

questions.q: One wheat plant can give you...
questions.why: One plant gives many grains, so a little seed grows into a lot of food.

k_hay.name: Meadow hay
k_hay.desc: Grass, cut and dried, keeps for the whole winter.
k_hay.topic: Grass grows fast in a meadow; farmers cut it, let it dry in the sun and store it as hay; hay is soft bedding and winter food for animals; fresh grass would rot, dry hay keeps.
k_hay.page: Grass grows quickly in a meadow. A farmer cuts it and lets it dry in the sun. Dry grass is called hay. It does not rot, so it keeps for the whole winter. Hay makes soft beds and good food for hutches and pens. Keep some hay back, and you can sow more.

questions.q: What is hay?
answers: Grass that was cut and dried
questions.why: Hay is grass that was cut and dried in the sun.

questions.q: Why do farmers dry grass into hay?
questions.why: Fresh grass rots, dry hay keeps for months.

questions.q: What is hay good for?
answers: Soft beds and feed for animals
questions.why: Hay makes a soft bed and is food for animals.

k_winter_wheat.name: Winter wheat
k_winter_wheat.desc: Some wheat is sown in autumn and ripens after the winter.
k_winter_wheat.topic: Winter wheat is sown in autumn; it sprouts, rests under the cold and snow, and grows again in spring; it ripens earlier than spring wheat and gives more grain; summer wheat is sown in spring.
k_winter_wheat.page: Most wheat is sown in spring. But there is also winter wheat. A farmer sows it in autumn. It sprouts, then rests under the cold and the snow, and grows again when spring comes. Because it started early, it gives more grain. You can only sow it in autumn or winter.

questions.q: When do farmers sow winter wheat?
questions.why: Winter wheat is sown in autumn and rests through the winter.

questions.q: What does winter wheat do in the cold?
questions.why: It rests under the cold and snow and grows again in spring.

questions.q: Why does winter wheat give more grain?
questions.why: An early start gives the plant more time to grow grain.

k_sleep.name: Sleep
k_sleep.desc: Sleep lets body and mind recover.
k_sleep.topic: Sleep lets the body rest and grow and the brain sort out what it learned; children need about nine to eleven hours; a dark, quiet, comfortable bed helps; tired people make more mistakes.
k_sleep.page: When you sleep, your body rests and grows, and your brain sorts out everything you learned that day. Children need about nine to eleven hours of sleep. A dark, quiet room and a comfy bed help a lot. A tired farmer makes more mistakes.

questions.q: What does sleep do for you?
answers: It lets your body rest and your brain sort what you learned
It makes you taller in one night
It uses up all your energy
questions.why: Sleep lets the body rest and grow, and the brain sorts out what you learned.

questions.q: What helps you sleep well?
answers: A dark, quiet room and a comfy bed
questions.why: A dark, quiet room and a comfy bed make it easy to fall asleep.

questions.q: What happens when you are very tired?
questions.why: Tired people make more mistakes and have less energy.

k_food.name: A colourful plate
k_food.desc: Different foods give your body different things.
k_food.topic: Different foods give the body different things it needs: grains give energy, vegetables and fruit give vitamins, beans, eggs and milk help the body grow; eating many colours and many kinds is healthy.
k_food.page: Different foods give your body different things. Bread and porridge give you energy. Vegetables and fruit give vitamins. Beans, eggs and milk help your body grow. So a good plate has many kinds and many colours, and not always the same dish.

questions.q: Why is it good to eat many different foods?
answers: Different foods give your body different things
Because one food is always enough
Because it makes the plate heavier
questions.why: Each food gives the body something different, so variety keeps you healthy.

questions.q: Which food gives you energy for a long morning?
questions.why: Grains like porridge and bread give lasting energy.

questions.q: How do you make a meal healthier?
questions.why: Colourful vegetables add vitamins and fibre to a meal.

k_strength.name: Strong muscles
k_strength.desc: Muscles get stronger when you use them.
k_strength.topic: Muscles get stronger when they are used again and again; after hard work they need rest and food to grow; stretching and warming up before heavy work helps; lift with the legs, not the back.
k_strength.page: Muscles get stronger when you use them again and again. After hard work they need rest and good food to grow. Before heavy work, stretch a little to warm up. And when you lift something heavy, bend your knees and use your legs, not your back.

questions.q: How do muscles get stronger?
answers: By being used again and again
questions.why: Using muscles regularly, with enough rest and food, makes them stronger.

questions.q: What do muscles need after hard work?
questions.why: Muscles grow stronger during rest, when they have good food.

questions.q: How should you lift something heavy?
answers: Bend your knees and use your legs
Bend over and pull with your back
questions.why: Using your legs protects your back.

k_friends.name: Friends
k_friends.desc: Helping others feels good, for them and for you.
k_friends.topic: Helping others and being kind makes the helper and the helped feel good; friends share heavy work and share joy; a good friend listens, shares and says thank you.
k_friends.page: Being kind and helping others makes them feel good, and you too. Friends share heavy work, and they share fun. A good friend listens, shares and says thank you. On a farm, many hands make a big job small.

questions.q: How do you often feel after you helped a friend?
questions.why: Helping others makes people feel good too.

questions.q: What does a good friend do?
answers: Listens, shares and says thank you
questions.why: Listening, sharing and being thankful make friendships strong.

questions.q: Why are friends useful on a farm?
answers: Many hands make a big job small
questions.why: Friends share heavy work, so it gets done faster.

k_calm.name: Calm and breathing
k_calm.desc: A slow breath and a short break calm you down.
k_calm.topic: When you feel worried or rushed, slow breathing calms the body: in slowly through the nose, out slowly through the mouth; a short break, a walk or looking at nature helps; people who never take breaks get tired and cranky.
k_calm.page: When you feel worried or rushed, you can calm down. Breathe in slowly through your nose, and out slowly through your mouth. A short break, a walk or looking at the trees helps too. A farmer who never takes a break gets tired and cranky.

questions.q: What can you do when you feel worried or rushed?
answers: Breathe slowly and take a short break
questions.why: Slow breathing and a short pause calm the body down.

questions.q: How do you breathe to calm down?
answers: Hold your breath for a long time
questions.why: Slow, steady breaths tell your body it is safe to relax.

questions.q: What happens if you never take a break?
questions.why: Without breaks people get tired and in a bad mood.

k_play.name: Play and music
k_play.desc: Play, music and drawing are good for you.
k_play.topic: Play, music and drawing help the body relax and the mind be creative; fun is not wasted time, because rested and happy people learn and work better afterwards.
k_play.page: Play, music and drawing help you relax and be creative. Having fun is not a waste of time. People who play and rest learn better and work better afterwards. So make some music, draw a picture or play a game with a friend.

questions.q: Why is play good for you?
answers: It helps you relax and be creative
It uses up all the day
questions.why: Play relaxes the mind and helps you think of new things.

questions.q: Which of these is play?
answers: Drawing or making music for fun
questions.why: Drawing and making music for fun are play.

questions.q: Is playing a waste of time?
answers: No, it helps you work better afterwards
questions.why: Rested and happy people learn and work better.

k_regrow.name: Take only what grows back
k_regrow.desc: The forest gives, but it needs time to give again.
k_regrow.topic: A forest gives wood, sticks and clay; trees grow back from saplings but slowly; if you take more than grows back, there is less and less; taking only what grows back keeps the forest alive for ever.
k_regrow.page: The forest gives you sticks, wood and clay. A felled tree leaves a stump, and from the stump a young tree can grow, but that takes a long time. If you take more than grows back, there is less and less. If you take only what grows back, the forest stays alive for ever. Look at how it is doing before you take more.

questions.q: What happens if you cut more trees than grow back?
answers: There are fewer and fewer trees
questions.why: Trees need a long time to grow, so cutting too many leaves the forest bare.

questions.q: How can a forest give wood for ever?
answers: By taking only what grows back
questions.why: If you take only as much as grows back, the forest never runs out.

questions.q: What grows from a stump or a seed in the forest?
questions.why: A sapling is a young tree, and it needs many years to become big.
